Lead Story · EU Circular Economy · Ecodesign
EU Ecodesign Regulation triggers on 19 July: digital product passports launch and destroying unsold consumer goods becomes illegal
Two of the most consequential rules under Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 on the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products (ESPR) begin applying on 19 July 2026: the ban on destruction of unsold consumer goods and the framework for mandatory digital product passports for regulated product groups.

The destruction ban applies to large companies handling unsold consumer products, targeting the routine incineration or landfilling of unsold textiles, footwear, and other consumer goods that has become characteristic of fast fashion and volume retail. Large companies must publicly disclose annually the quantities and categories of unsold products they discard, together with the reasons and the fate of those goods (donation, recycling, remanufacturing, or destruction where unavoidable). Micro and small companies are exempt; medium-sized companies benefit from a six-year transition. Sector-specific delegated acts will extend the destruction ban to further product groups over time.

The digital product passport (DPP) framework establishes the legal architecture for machine-readable product-level information covering material composition, recyclability, repairability, carbon footprint, and supply-chain provenance. The Commission has committed to establishing a central registry for digital product passports by 19 July 2026. The first sectoral delegated acts, expected to prioritise textiles, iron and steel, electronics, and batteries, will define the specific data points, formats, and access rules for each product group. DPPs will not appear on shelves immediately: the delegated acts and the underlying data infrastructure need to be built out over 2026 to 2028 before physical products carry compliant passports.

The 19 July date is a legal milestone, not a consumer-facing launch. But it sets the calendar for the sectoral rollouts that follow, and it activates the disclosure and destruction rules that apply immediately to companies in scope. The ESPR is the operational core of the EU Circular Economy Act package due later in 2026 and a foundational element of the Clean Industrial Deal’s target of doubling Europe’s circular material use rate to 24% by 2030 (currently 12.2%).

Why it matters: For sustainability, procurement, and product teams at large consumer brands, 19 July marks the point where product-lifecycle disclosure becomes an operational, not preparatory, workstream. The destruction-disclosure rule is the near-term compliance surface; the DPP infrastructure is the medium-term architecture. Both require data flows that most companies do not yet have.
Sources: European Commission, DG Environment · Ecomondo · European Commission

Regulatory & Policy Watch
EU Repair Directive · Consumer Rights · Circular Economy
Repair Directive applies from 31 July: manufacturers must repair regulated goods within a reasonable time and price

Directive (EU) 2024/1799 on common rules promoting the repair of goods, the Repair Directive, applies from 31 July 2026. From that date, producers of goods subject to reparability requirements under EU law (including washing machines, dishwashers, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners, mobile phones, tablets, and servers) must repair those goods within a reasonable time and price, both within and outside the legal guarantee period. Consumers gain a new right to request repair; producers may not obstruct independent repair, refuse repair of used or refurbished products, or use contractual clauses or software techniques to prevent repair by third parties.

Member States must set up at least one national online repair platform enabling consumers to compare repairers, refurbishers, and sellers of refurbished goods. The Commission is also developing a voluntary European Repair Information Form, a standardised quote template designed to make prices comparable across service providers. Extension of the legal guarantee period by 12 months is triggered where a consumer opts for repair rather than replacement of a faulty good under warranty.

Why it matters: The Repair Directive sits alongside the Ecodesign Regulation and the incoming Circular Economy Act as the operational scaffold for a mandatory-repair economy. For product teams at manufacturers in scope, the 31 July trigger requires reviewed spare-part policies, software update commitments, and repairer-access documentation, not just marketing copy.
Sources: European Commission · EUR-Lex
EFRAG · ESRS · Transition Plan
EFRAG launches consultation on the ESRS Transition Plan standard, published on 23 July after SRB approval on 1 July

The EFRAG Sustainability Reporting Board approved the draft ESRS on Transition Plans for Climate Change Mitigation (ESRS-TC) on 1 July 2026, ahead of a formal public consultation opening on 23 July. The Commission requested a dedicated transition-plan standard under the Omnibus I simplification package to reduce fragmentation between the CSRD transition-plan requirement, the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive transition-plan obligation, the EU Climate Law, and the Capital Requirements Directive. ESRS-TC is designed to provide a single set of disclosure requirements that satisfies all four bases.

EFRAG intends to publish the draft standard for a comment period of at least 60 days. The Commission expects to adopt ESRS-TC as a separate delegated act in 2027, alongside the sector-specific standards. Companies subject to the CSRD, and financial institutions using the CRD-transition-plan basis, should treat the consultation as the last meaningful window to shape the disclosure architecture before the standard is finalised.

Why it matters: For corporate sustainability teams already scoping transition plans under existing ESRS E1 requirements, ESRS-TC is the standard that will govern the durable format. Financial institutions with prudential transition-plan obligations under CRD 6 also gain a common data spine. Both cohorts should engage during the consultation window: interoperability decisions taken now will shape reporting cost for the rest of the decade.
Sources: EFRAG · Linklaters Sustainable Futures
EuGB Regulation · ESMA · External Reviewers
European Green Bond Regulation: transitional regime for external reviewers ended 22 June, ESMA register is now the sole gateway

The transitional regime under Articles 69 and 70 of the European Green Bond (EuGB) Regulation ended on 22 June this year. External review firms that were operating under the transitional register may no longer issue pre- or post-issuance reviews of European Green Bonds. Only firms formally authorised by ESMA and published on the ESMA register may act as external reviewers going forward, and they are now subject to ongoing ESMA supervision, including conduct-of-business, conflicts-of-interest, and disclosure rules.

Issuers preparing EuGB-labelled bonds should verify their reviewer’s ESMA status before commissioning any new review. Reviews issued after 22 June by non-authorised firms are not valid for EuGB compliance. The change is the culmination of the 18-month transitional window that began on 21 December 2024.

Why it matters: The EuGB label is the only voluntary EU-supervised green bond standard tied directly to the Taxonomy. For sustainable finance teams at issuers and investors, the closure of the transitional regime is the point at which reviewer selection becomes a supervised-market decision, not a market-choice decision.
Sources: ESMA · European Commission
In brief
SFDR 2.0 · European Parliament · ECON
SFDR 2.0: European Parliament ECON committee scheduled to vote on Gerbrandy draft on 15 July

The Economic and Monetary Affairs (ECON) committee of the European Parliament is scheduled to vote on 15 July 2026 on rapporteur Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy’s draft report on the SFDR review. The draft supports the Commission’s move toward a simplified three-category product framework (Sustainable, Transition, ESG Basics) and raises the bar for products claiming environmental or social characteristics through mandatory Principal Adverse Indicators reporting and quantitative investment thresholds. The full Parliament plenary is expected to endorse Parliament’s position after the summer recess, opening the door to trilogue negotiations with the Council in the autumn.

Sources: IPE · HSF Kramer
EU ETS · Climate Package · Commission Proposal
Commission ETS revision proposal expected 17 July: free allocation, removals integration, and cap trajectory in scope

The European Commission is expected to publish its EU Emissions Trading System revision proposal around 17 July 2026, the first substantive reform since the 2023 Fit for 55 package. The proposal is expected to cover the Linear Reduction Factor for the post-2030 cap (currently 4.4%, with EPP voices pushing lower and Poland pushing lower still), free allocation rules in light of the CBAM downstream expansion, integration of permanent carbon removals into the compliance framework, and Market Stability Reserve calibration. The proposal will kick off Parliament and Council negotiations expected to conclude in Q1 2027.

Sources: OPIS · Carbon Pulse

Market & Corporate Moves
JBS · Food and Agriculture · Scope 3
JBS drops 2040 net-zero target and removes all Scope 3 goals in its 2025 Non-Financial Disclosure Report

JBS NV, the world’s largest meatpacker, published its Non-Financial Disclosure Report for 2025 on 8 July 2026 and formally abandoned its 2040 net-zero commitment. The report removes all Scope 3 emissions targets, including the value-chain reductions covering the livestock that JBS slaughters and the feed and land-use emissions embedded in its supply chain. Scope 3 accounts for the overwhelming majority of the group’s greenhouse gas footprint: Scope 1 and 2 combined represented roughly 4% of the total in 2025. The company also drops its previously announced $100 million research and development investment target aimed at Scope 3 abatement.

What remains is narrower and operational: a 30% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions across core operations by 2030, and a 70% reduction by 2050, both against a 2019 baseline. The company cited “immense” execution challenges on Scope 3 and pointed to factors outside its direct control. The retreat follows a 2025 settlement with the New York Attorney General, which had accused JBS of making misleading environmental claims tied to the earlier 2040 pledge; JBS settled for $1.1 million without admitting wrongdoing.

Why it matters: JBS is the largest publicly listed emitter to formally walk back Scope 3. Under SBTi V2.0’s revised architecture, target-setting must still be aligned with sector pathways for large emitters, but the standard now recognises “best efforts” framings. JBS’s move is a market test of how far a heavyweight can retreat from Scope 3 without triggering investor, insurer, or regulatory consequences. For anyone modelling food-and-agri decarbonisation trajectories, treat this as a negative demand signal for value-chain financing and abatement infrastructure.
Sources: ESG Today · ESG Dive · edie
Greentech & Cleantech
Fusion · Series A · Cleantech Financing
Focused Energy raises $240 million Series A for laser inertial fusion, backed by Lowercarbon, RWE, and the European Innovation Council Fund

German-American laser inertial fusion startup Focused Energy closed a $240 million Series A round in the week of 6 to 10 July 2026, backed by Lowercarbon Capital, RWE, Germany’s innovation agency SPRIND, the European Innovation Council Fund, Prime Movers Lab, and other investors. The financing supports scaling of Focused Energy’s laser-based inertial confinement approach, which follows the ignition milestone achieved by the National Ignition Facility in 2022. Focused Energy’s pilot plant plans target a demonstration facility by the early 2030s.

Alongside Focused Energy, Paris-based RGreen Invest closed EUR 500 million ($572 million) for its fourth Infrabridge infrastructure debt fund, targeting Europe’s energy transition. Together the two closes point to a return of institutional appetite for both deep-tech energy R&D and mature European infrastructure debt, after the softer 2024 to 2025 cleantech funding environment.

Why it matters: Fusion is not a decade-relevant supply-side option, but private capital is once again committing multi-year, multi-hundred-million-euro tickets to it. For sustainability strategy teams tracking long-horizon technology optionality, and for asset owners weighting energy-transition exposure, watch the Series B round terms and the demonstration-plant timelines as the credible near-term signal.
Sources: ImpactAlpha Dealflow · Focused Energy
AI & Sustainability
Microsoft · Environmental Report · AI Infrastructure
Microsoft’s 2026 Environmental Sustainability Report: emissions up 25% in FY2025, purchased-electricity emissions restated as AI buildout accelerates

Microsoft published its 2026 Environmental Sustainability Report on 9 July 2026. Total greenhouse gas emissions for the fiscal year ending 30 June 2025 reached approximately 20 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent, up 25% year on year from roughly 16 million tonnes in FY2024. Emissions intensity rose to about 75 tCO2e per million dollars of revenue, from 68 in the previous year. The company attributed the increase primarily to the expansion of AI data centre infrastructure, including embodied emissions from data-centre construction and the associated grid electricity consumption.

The report also reflects a methodological shift: Microsoft has moved away from relying on renewable energy certificates unbundled from underlying generation and toward power purchase agreements that finance additional carbon-free capacity. The reclassification, which better reflects actual grid impact, produced a large restated increase in reported Scope 2 market-based emissions from purchased electricity between FY2024 and FY2025. Microsoft was explicit in the accompanying blog post: “While AI infrastructure is driving demand for energy, water, land, and materials, sustainability solutions are not scaling fast enough to meet demand.” The company reiterated its 2030 carbon-negative goal while acknowledging the trajectory is now materially harder.

Why it matters: Alongside Google’s 2026 report (Scope 3 up 25%, moonshot “getting harder”, covered in Issue 09), Microsoft’s numbers confirm the Big Tech pattern: operational abatement and clean-power procurement are being outpaced by AI compute buildout. For investors, insurers, and corporate customers relying on hyperscaler climate commitments as a Scope 3 assumption, that assumption needs revising. The methodological shift on Scope 2 accounting is also material: additionality-based procurement is now the credible standard, and legacy REC-based zero-emission claims should be treated with growing scepticism.
Sources: Microsoft on the Issues · Microsoft 2026 Environmental Sustainability Report · Carbon Pulse

Science & Data Signals
Copernicus C3S · Ocean Warming · Marine Heatwaves
Warmest June on record for global sea surface temperature; marine heatwaves cover 82% of the world’s oceans by month-end

The Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) reported on 9 July 2026 that June 2026 was the warmest June on record for global average sea surface temperature (SST), with the extra-polar ocean (60°S to 60°N) exceeding the previous June record set in 2024 by 0.01°C. On 30 June the global SST anomaly reached +0.5°C, the highest value ever recorded for that date. The tropical Pacific set its warmest June on record at 27.26°C average SST, surpassing the 26.90°C set in 2023. On land, western Europe endured its hottest June ever, driven by a persistent heat dome.

By month-end, marine heatwave conditions covered approximately 82% of the world’s oceans, per Copernicus Marine (CMEMS) satellite analysis. The first half of 2026 has been marked by persistent ocean warmth and expanding marine heatwaves across the Mediterranean, North Atlantic, and tropical Pacific, with ecosystem consequences for pelagic fisheries and coastal biodiversity still being assessed.

Why it matters: June 2026 is the operational data point behind the physical risk assumptions that underpin CSRD climate risk disclosures, TCFD scenario analyses, and TNFD ocean-dependency assessments this reporting cycle. Marine heatwaves at 82% coverage are outside the historical envelope used to calibrate most fisheries, insurance, and food-system risk models. For companies with material exposure to seafood supply chains or coastal operations, the number should trigger a physical-risk model review.
Sources: Copernicus C3S · Copernicus Marine · Euronews
Social Impact & Just Transition
FRLD · Loss and Damage · Climate Finance
Loss and Damage Fund ninth board meeting in Manila: $2 to 3 billion in requests, $250 million available, first project approvals slip to end of year

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) held its ninth board meeting at the Asian Development Bank headquarters in Manila from 8 to 10 July 2026. The Barbados Implementation Modalities (BIM) funding call, which closed at the end of June, drew requests totalling approximately US$2 to 3 billion against the US$250 million currently available in the startup phase. The board had originally aimed to approve the first tranche of projects by end-June 2026; that target has now slipped to the end of 2026, with the board citing the volume of proposals and the need to finalise screening and approval procedures.

Board co-chair Richard Sherman said discussions covered a resource mobilisation strategy aimed at converting COP28 Dubai pledges into binding agreements. The gap between requests and available resources exposes the structural constraint on operationalising loss-and-damage finance three and a half years after the fund’s creation was announced at COP27.

Why it matters: For sustainability and climate risk practitioners engaging with adaptation and loss-and-damage as material topics under ESRS E1, TCFD physical risk, and TNFD community-dependency disclosures, the FRLD scale-up trajectory is the key indicator of whether international public finance will materially participate in the adaptation gap. Ten-to-one over-subscription with a delayed disbursement is not encouraging.
Sources: Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage · Eco-Business · Loss and Damage Collaboration
Excellent News
New Zealand’s kākāpō has its best breeding season on record: 100+ chicks hatched from a population of just 235 adults
The kākāpō, the world’s only flightless parrot and one of its rarest birds, completed its most successful breeding season on record in 2026, with more than 100 chicks hatched from a founder population of 235 adult birds. The tally beats the previous best of 85 chicks recorded in 2019. The Department of Conservation’s Kākāpō Recovery team attributes the result to a combination of a strong rimu mast (the tree fruit that triggers kākāpō breeding), intensive nest management, and the species’ steady expansion across predator-free islands. Every chick brings the population an increment closer to genetic and demographic security, in a recovery programme that has spent 30 years pulling the kākāpō back from the edge. For anyone in need of proof that patient, well-resourced conservation science works, the kākāpō is the standing example.
Positive News · DOC Kākāpō Recovery

Tool of the week
EFRAG VSME Digital Template & XBRL Taxonomy: the practical way to answer value-chain sustainability data requests

With the 3 July 2026 adoption of the revised ESRS and the parallel Voluntary Standard for smaller companies (VSME), EFRAG’s VSME Digital Template & XBRL Taxonomy becomes the operational tool for two audiences at once: SMEs outside CSRD scope that want a proportionate reporting framework, and CSRD-scoped companies that need a standardised way to collect sustainability data from their value chains. The critical constraint enshrined in the revised ESRS is that CSRD reporters cannot demand more information from value-chain partners than what the VSME covers. The digital template makes that limit machine-readable.

The toolkit is free. It bundles an Excel-based reporting template that walks through the VSME data points, an XBRL taxonomy that produces machine-readable filings compatible with the European Single Electronic Format (ESEF), and an open-source converter that generates the XBRL output from the completed Excel file. For consultants supporting SME clients, and for procurement and supplier-engagement teams building ESRS-compliant supplier surveys, it is the fastest route to a defensible, standard-aligned dataset. EFRAG plans to extend the digital toolkit alongside the ESRS-TC and XBRL taxonomy consultations expected across mid to late 2026.

Careers
Green Skills · LinkedIn · Sustainability Hiring
Green hiring outpaces green skills supply: sustainability roles command a 54.6% hiring premium as green demand outstrips training

Recent labour-market analyses published in July 2026 show that workers with green skills enjoy a hiring rate about 54.6% higher than those without, with the gap widening over 2021 to 2025. Green hiring grew roughly twice as fast as green skills supply over the same period, with the UK among the markets where demand runs meaningfully ahead of the trained talent pool. The composition of green hiring has shifted too: more than half of green hires now sit in traditionally non-green job titles (operations, procurement, technology, finance), reflecting how sustainability has embedded across the corporate stack rather than remaining in dedicated ESG teams.

Demand is concentrated in ESG reporting, climate risk, sustainable finance, decarbonisation, circular economy, and renewable energy development. On the international policy side, the ILO and the Nigerian government launched the second phase of the Social Dimension of Ecological Transition Project on 2 July 2026, a five-year programme (2025 to 2029) translating climate commitments into skills, enterprise support, and social protection investments. Job boards to bookmark for the European market include Trellis (formerly GreenBiz), EuroClimateJobs, and Enable.Green.

Why it matters: For sustainability leads, the shift of green hiring into non-green job titles is the practical form of the “every function is a sustainability function” argument, and it changes the internal case for upskilling and cross-functional secondments. For consultants and freelancers, the 54.6% hiring premium and the CSRD/ESRS-driven surge in reporting demand mean the near-term contract market is tighter than the general labour market suggests.
Sources: Sustainability Magazine · International Labour Organization
